item.description:
All supporting acts quit Ed Sheeran tour in protest of Macklemore’s removal

Submitted by Bilge Kotan on Wed, 09/16/2026 - 00:01
Four supporting acts, including musician Finneas, stood in solidarity with the US rapper, as Sheeran said the rapper's removal was not his decision
Finneas O'Connell attends the 2025 LACMA Art+Film Gala at Los Angeles County Museum of Art on 1 November 2025 in Los Angeles, California (Frazer Harrison / Getty Images via AFP)
Off

The artist Finneas and three other supporting acts quit Ed Sheeran's tour on Tuesday, after the US rapper Macklemore was removed for his pro-Palestine comments on stage.

Finneas, Irish acts Aaron Rowe and Beoga, and Lukas Graham of Denmark all posted statements announcing they were quitting Sheeran's "Loop Tour" in solidarity with the rapper and Palestinian people.

"Artists must not be silenced when they speak up for the oppressed,” Finneas said in a statement on social media.

His statement came after Irish singer Aaron Rowe published a statement, announcing that he had decided to withdraw as a support act for the British singer.

"Ed has been a friend to me and has changed my life," he said. "But as Irish people we know all too well about genocide, forced famine and violent occupation. I cannot stand by and allow billionaires to use their position of power to silence the rightful voices of those who speak up against Israeli genocide and who highlight the savage murder of children."

The Irish band Beoga echoed a similar sentiment in a social media post, as they announced departing the tour ın response to what they called "silencing of Macklemore by zionist lobbies”. 

The Danish pop band Lukas Graham also announced their departure from the remaining acts,

"We should be able to speak about war, about civilians being killed, about children who deserve to grow up," teh lead singer of the band said.

"Nobody’s bank balance should decide who gets to speak or which suffering we’re allowed to acknowledge.”

On 4 September, during his opening performance, Macklemore called for a “Free Palestine” during a two-minute speech before performing his pro-Palestine anthem "Hind’s Hall", named after five-year-old Hind Rajab, who was shot and killed by Israeli forces in Gaza in 2024. His speech drew both praise and backlash from across the political spectrum.

The pro-Israeli group Israeli American Council (IAC) launched a petition to pressure Sheeran to drop Macklemore as his opening act from future tour dates following the speech.

In a detailed statement on Monday, the US rapper announced that “Ed Sheeran and his team” removed him from the tour after billionaire Robert Kraft rallied other stadium owners to threaten Sheeran with blocking him from using their stadiums if he didn't drop him.

Sheeran defended himself in a statement, saying that "Macklemore coming off tour was the promoter's decision, it was not mine."

Some fans took to social media criticising the singer for not taking a stance and pointing out other instances he used his platform to raise awareness on other political issues.

The British pop star also rejected the criticism that he was "complicit"; he has his personal views on what he called a "devastating conflict", and he does not use his professional platform for politics.

"Just because I choose not to speak publicly, it doesn't mean I dont have them and it deosn't mean I don't care," he said.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Gaza: Dozens trapped under rubble after Israeli-hit building collapses
item.description:
Gaza: Dozens trapped under rubble after Israeli-hit building collapses

Submitted by Maha Hussaini on Wed, 09/16/2026 - 08:29
Rescue crews race to reach residents as the death toll rises in western Gaza City
People gather as Civil Defence workers attempt to rescue those who are trapped beneath the rubble of a residential building that had been damaged in an earlier Israeli strike during the war and collapsed on Wednesday, in Gaza City, 16 September 2026 (Reuters/Mahmoud Issa)
Off

A building in Gaza previously hit by Israeli forces collapsed on Wednesday, killing at least 14 people as dozens more remained trapped under the rubble, including dozens of children.

The Palestinian Civil Defence, Gaza's emergency and rescue agency, said the six-storey residential building on al-Sinaa Street in western Gaza City collapsed suddenly while residents were sleeping inside.

More than 10 families, totalling around 80 people, lived in the building, according to residents. Dozens were children.

Civil Defence teams recovered the bodies of 14 people, including five children, and rescued 10 injured people.

Mahmoud Basal, the Civil Defence spokesperson, said emergency workers could hear the cries of people trapped beneath the rubble and were doing everything they could to reach them.

Abdullah al-Majdalawi, director of public relations and media at Gaza's Civil Defence, said rescue teams had been working continuously since the collapse.

"Every victim we have pulled from beneath the rubble appears to have been sleeping on a mattress. They were asleep when the building collapsed," Majdalawi told Middle East Eye.

But rescue teams lack the heavy machinery needed to reach those trapped, with much of Gaza's equipment destroyed by Israel during the genocide.

"We lack even the most basic tools," Majdalawi said.

"In the first moments after the collapse, we had to ask neighbours and displaced people nearby to bring hammers, shovels and other tools because of the severe shortage of equipment," he added.

🚨 BREAKING : Children are crying for help from beneath the rubble in the middle of the night after a residential building collapsed on six families sheltering inside after it had been previously damaged by Israeli bombardment. More than six families remain trapped under the debris. Rescue teams are desperately trying to reach them in extremely difficult conditions.

— Gaza Notifications (@gazanotice) September 16, 2026

Talal al-Harazin, 53, a displaced Palestinian who lived in a tent metres from the building, said the collapse felt like an "earthquake".

"At around 3:10 am, the entire building collapsed. It took less than 10 seconds for the building to come down," he told Middle East Eye.

Harazin said around 10 families were living in the building, including the Abu Ras, al-Swatri, Adas, al-Jaabari, al-Ajla and Saada families. The smallest family had around 10 members, most of them women and children.

Harazin said the building had been hit and damaged by Israeli bombardment and had already sunk about three floors into the ground. But the families had nowhere else to live.

"Unfortunately, we expected it to collapse. People had warned them, but they said, ‘Where can we live?’" he said.

"Pieces of the building were falling every day. Just yesterday, stones fell from it, and we said it could collapse. And that same night, it collapsed."

'On the verge of a real disaster'

The collapsed building was among an estimated 2,000 buildings across the Gaza Strip at risk of collapse because of damage caused by Israeli strikes.

Despite the danger, many of the buildings remain inhabited by large numbers of residents who have run out of other shelter.

Majdalawi said residents were forced to use the collapsed building despite knowing it was cracked, as they had nowhere else to go.

"This is a recurring situation. Buildings at risk of collapse are becoming graves for their residents. The only difference is the timing," he warned.

'Buildings at risk of collapse are becoming graves for their residents'

- Abdullah al-Majdalawi, Gaza's Civil Defence

"Dozens of homes have collapsed, and dozens of people have been killed in this way."

He also warned of the added risks posed by the approaching winter.

"We are now on the verge of a real disaster as winter approaches. If mobile homes, caravans and reconstruction materials are not brought into Gaza, we will see more of these disasters."

During Israel's genocide in Gaza, which began in 2023, Israeli forces damaged or destroyed an estimated 90 percent of housing units in the territory, according to the UN. 

Almost the entire population of 2.2 million people has been internally displaced during the war. 

A report released last month by the Shelter Cluster, led by the Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC), found that an estimated 1.98 million Palestinians in Gaza - 94 percent of the population – need shelter and basic household assistance.

A ceaefire signed in October last year was intended to end the Israeli genocide, by halting attacks against Palestinians, allowing the flow of aid into Gaza, including shelter materials, and paving the way for reconstruction.

However, Israel has repeatedly violated the US-mediated agreement, conducting near-daily attacks, restricting reconstruction efforts, and blocking the entry of much of the aid needed in Gaza, inclduing shelter material.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Life on the edge in Lebanon: The psychological toll of living along Israel's 'Yellow Line'
item.description:
Life on the edge in Lebanon: The psychological toll of living along Israel's 'Yellow Line'

Submitted by Tamara Davison on Wed, 09/16/2026 - 09:05
Medics supporting Lebanese with homes just beside the unilaterally drawn Israeli boundary say requests for psychological support are ‘increasing chronically’
A warning of 'enemy' marks Ghandouriyeh’s outskirts, just beyond Israel’s Yellow Line in south Lebanon, on 28 August 2026 (Tamara Davison/MEE)
Off

Mariam Ismail Ballout sat at the entrance of a mobile medical clinic in Ghandouriyeh in south Lebanon, waiting to speak to a doctor. 

Outside the clinic, most of the surrounding homes in the small hilltop village, a strategic position Israel previously tried to occupy, have either been severely damaged or completely flattened by strikes earlier this year.

“All our houses are ruined, all our houses are on the ground, demolished,” the 66-year-old told Middle East Eye while waiting to collect her medicine.

“My house burned down, meaning there's no washing machine, no refrigerator, nothing. There's no gas, nothing.” 

She paused, suddenly overwhelmed with tears. 

Located just south of Froun, one of the designated “pilot zones” established in Lebanon’s Nabatieh governorate, Ghandouriyeh sits just outside of Israel’s imposed “Yellow Line”. But the situation here is far from stable.

A rolling green valley known as Wadi al-Hujeir divides the village from a direct line of sight of the Israeli military presence on the other side. A large plastic bin surrounded by rocks, signposted with the warning of “enemy” beyond in Arabic, is all that separates the outskirts of the town from now-inaccessible roads ahead. 

Roughly 228 families have returned to their homes in Ghandouriyeh despite the quiet village lacking any running water or electricity, said mayor Mohammed Ali Nader. Many had few options other than to live among the shells of their homes and share buildings with neighbours, as they cannot afford to rent elsewhere. 

There has not been a direct strike on the village in “months” the mayor told MEE, but residents here live in a constant state of high alert that medical specialists warn is having a profound impact on people’s mental health.

Critical lifeline

“Some people with no history of previous mental health disorders are now having symptoms of mental health disorders,” Medecins Sans Frontieres (MSF) counsellor and clinical psychologist Almas Al Andary, 33, told MEE from the mobile clinic. 

MSF runs daily mobile medical units across parts of south Lebanon, serving as a critical lifeline for villages often left with little access to nearby healthcare.

‘We definitely see a lot of people having acute stress disorders. And these symptoms we can't formally diagnose because the crisis is still ongoing’

- Almas Al Andary, MSF psychologist

According to the organisation’s records, counsellors have held 1,326 individual mental health sessions in southern Lebanon since the war started on 2 March, with teams confirming requests for psychological support across the region are “increasing chronically”. 

When Ballout arrived at the MSF clinic in Ghandouriyeh on 28 August, the persistent whirr of an Israeli drone was hanging over the village, a sound that residents say has become a near-daily occurrence here. 

“I’m afraid of the drones,” the grandmother of 14 told MEE. Often, residents hear the buzzing sound but are unable to actually see the drones watching them. 

On this particular day, only three people attended the clinic while MEE was on the ground, which medical staff say was unusually low. Yet of those who did attend, two were new patients seeking mental health support. 

“Today the number decreased because yesterday there were air strikes and people fled again from this area,” Al Andary said. 

The psychologist explained that a lot of mental health cases she has recently supported have been prompted by this year’s conflict, as well as the ongoing threat of instability and displacement, the loss of homes, livelihoods and loved ones. 

Despite a US-brokered ceasefire announced this June in Lebanon, Israel continues to fire beyond the yellow line into districts including Nabatieh and Tyre, claiming dozens of lives.

In south Lebanon, Israeli drones use the sound of crying children to lure civilians
Read More »

The Lebanese Army last week confirmed it had “intensified operations” in southern areas currently not under occupation amid signs of escalating tensions. 

“We definitely see a lot of people having acute stress disorders. And these symptoms we can't formally diagnose because the crisis is still ongoing,” Al Andary explained. 

“We find these symptoms where people are having intense responses to the drones or the air strikes, like tension, like hypervigilance, fear, constant worry.” 

Earlier this year, Embrace, a Lebanese mental health non-profit operating the country’s National Lifeline, revealed that call volume was 55 percent higher during the 2026 war compared to the 2024 conflict.

Yet little public data exists about the ongoing mental health situation in southern Lebanon amid fragile “ceasefire” conditions. On the ground, though, the reality is stark. 

“They are not sleeping well; there are a lot of sleep disorders, which are causing a lot of stress for them and causing a lot of them to take medications related to sleeping and to mental health conditions,” community health educator Farah Kerbaj told MEE. 

Medics such as the MSF’s midwife Reem Farhat say patients are often “very agitated”.

Stigma surrounding mental health and difficulty tracking data among displaced families may be compounding the situation.

Always ready to flee

Outside the municipal building where the MSF clinic is hosted, Ghandouriyeh’s mayor told MEE the village's most urgent need is access to water; without it, people cannot grow enough food to eat. 

But many families also appear ready to flee at a moment’s notice - a symptom likened to the hypervigilance that Al Andary describes. 

‘We're fed up, honestly. We're fed up with wars; we've had enough wars

- Mohammed Gannem, resident

“The people are coming back here,” Nader explains. “But any attack, they come running, they sit down in the valley at the intersection of the riverbank until the situation calms down.” 

Standing just outside the medical clinic, local resident Mohammed Gannem returned to the town with his family in June, relieved to find his home was still there, but still struggling: “Yesterday we didn't sleep,” he said. 

“We're fed up, honestly,” he told MEE. “We're fed up with wars; we've had enough wars.” 

He is also concerned about the psychological impact the situation is having on his two daughters. His youngest is almost two, and “she's become accustomed to the booming sound, and now when she hears booming, she gets scared”. 

Explanations about an increase in patients looking for psychological support may be twofold: people are potentially becoming more aware of mental health support in Lebanon and breaking away from former stigma, medics suggest, but also becoming more desperate. 

Speaking from Beirut’s southern suburbs where MSF was hosting another mobile clinic, counsellor Georges Jreij explains they see mental health cases in waves, one of which they’re expecting around the six-month mark of the war this month. 

Israel uses Lebanese civilians as bargaining chips

“It's usually the time it takes for the brain to really realise the situation, to be able to think about the stuff that people are going through,” he said. 

“And the central nervous system sort of calms down in these periods, so other sides of the brain are reactivated.” 

As the Ghandouriyeh health clinic session neared its end, another unexpected sound disrupted the town and briefly drowned out the drones above. 

A pale pink ice-cream van with a smashed windscreen slowly meandered past the rubble of homes, a rare hint of normalcy ringing out in playful jingles. 

But as the sound of the ice-cream van slowly faded across the hilltops, it was replaced once again with a menacing buzz of drones.
